### 1. execuTive summarY ##### IntroductIon copper prices embarked on an upward trend following the release of our previous report, rising to an intra-day high of $8,422/tonne in mid-september. This was driven by a series of announcements on fresh monetary loosening by major central banks which, combined with a weaker dollar, stimulated investor interest in the commodities sector. Thereafter, prices dipped back below $8,000/tonne in mid-October, and subsequently traded within a range of $7,500-$8,000/tonne up to the end of November, as investor appetite waned as the focus returned towards the sluggishness of global growth and concerns over the economic outlook. indeed, the eurozone debt crisis continues to dampen activity in that region, uncertainty surrounding the looming Us “fiscal cliff” has clouded the outlook for growth there, whilst fears over the health of chinese demand growth also served to weigh on prices. more recently, an easing of some of the aforementioned concerns surrounding chinese demand and positive data from the Us have provided support, and prices had rebounded from their lows to above $8,000/tonne in early December. From a fundamental perspective, the ongoing weakness in the economic environment has, ultimately, had an impact in restraining copper offtake. Within china, the evidence gathered from our latest research trip indicates that the expected second-half reboun

d in demand has been very slow to materialise, and bonded warehouse stocks have mushroomed as a result. consequently, whilst more recent economic data (see chapter 2) have provided some encouragement that the demand environment within the world’s largest consumer may see some improvement into the New Year, we have downgraded our forecasts for chinese demand. in a similar fashion, we have trimmed our growth projections for a host of other major consuming countries for this year and, in some cases, throughout the forecast period. Despite the demand-side weakness, we continue to project that the market will remain broadly balanced this year, as global production continues to underperform expectations. indeed, although there are signs that miners are ramping up output over the second half, we have revised our expectations as to the magnitude of this contribution. in addition to the underperformance of global mine production, a number of other factors have also helped to restrict the extent of the oversupply to the physical market amidst the weak demand environment. amongst these drivers has been lower price levels - average copper prices over the first eleven months of 2012 were 10.9% lower than those seen over the corresponding period of 2011 - which, in addition to sluggish industrial output in major economies over recent years, has restricted scrap supply to both producers (for production of secondary refined output) and consumers (for production of semi-fabricates by direct melting). in addition, although the shift in metal availability from the West to china has left the country well supplied, this trend, in addition to mounting problems in securing material from lme warehouses, has restricted material availability in the West. These factors have helped support spot premiums, and have restricted the downside for term premiums for next year, despite the weak demand environment. Nevertheless, with the market surplus remaining relatively small in terms of the overall market size, we are not forecasting a collapse in prices. in the final year of our forecast, we project average prices of $7,500/tonne, the lowest annual average price since 2010 but well in excess of the recent low of $5,164/tonne seen in 2009. ##### economIc AssumptIons The global economy has continued to slow this year due to sluggish growth and uncertainty in advanced countries, slowing growth in emerging market economies and the ongoing turmoil in europe. indeed, within europe, financial stress and recession in the peripheral eurozone nations have continued to spill into core northern economies, dragging the region into recession in the third quarter. meanwhile, whilst substantial improvements were seen in the United states in the third quarter of the year, notable headwinds still remain, perhaps the largest being the looming “fiscal cliff”. elsewhere, although economic performance in the major developing countries has remained relatively solid, the growth path has flattened as a result of a tightening of monetary and fiscal policies last year and a weak recovery in demand from advanced economies. and concerns over the fiscal cliff continue to breed uncertainty, improvements in the job and housing markets have recently buoyed sentiment. meanwhile, in china, recent indicators have provided encouragement that the economy is on track for a fourth-quarter rebound. There has been increasing growth in industrial production, and fixed asset investment and retail sales have also picked up in recent months. Under our Base case (45% probability), we expect a slowdown in world GDP growth this year to 2.0%, as a result of slowing economic activity in key developing countries, a fragile recovery in some major advanced economies and a continuing debt crisis in europe. Nevertheless, we are looking for an uptick in growth over the 2013-2015 period, to 2.7% on an average annual basis, with loose monetary policies remaining in place in key countries, together with the possible implementation of other global reflationary measures during this period. Under our more bullish scenario B (40% pro

bability), we expect to see a firmer global economic recovery compared with the Base case, with higher growth rates in both the major advanced and developing countries over the forecast period. We assume that the Us government and the Fed will implement further ultra-loose monetary and fiscal policies. We also expect the european central Bank (ecB) to take more aggressive measures to handle the debt crisis. The OecD leading indicators remained static for four consecutive months over July-October. The overall indicator for the eurozone slid in October and, whilst some indicators such as consumer confidence and the Pmi showed improvement in November, we remain cautious about the extent and sustainability of any recovery given weak underlying activity and high unemployment. in the United states, whilst Hurricane sandy dented manufacturing activity over the start of the fourth quarter in contrast, under our bearish scenario c with a 15% probability (down from 25% in the previous report), we assume that no further easing measures take place in the United states, while a faster pace of fiscal consolidation emerges in europe. as a result, world GDP growth is forecast to slow considerably this year and next and to remain subdued over the remainder of the outlook period, particularly in advanced economies. **4** 3-Year COPPer FOreCast - DeCember 2012 confidential - not for distribution

##### the dollAr after trading near four-month lows in mid-september, the Us dollar regained its strength against the euro in early October in response to upbeat Us economic data and continued to recover through to mid-November on renewed fears over the eurozone debt crisis. it has dropped recently on uncertainty surrounding the Us budget talks and ahead of the FOmc December meeting, where the Fed is expected to announce a new round of stimulus measures. The Us dollar is forecast to average $1.28/€ this year, compared with $1.39/€ seen in 2011. a further, yet slower, rise is expected in the following years, due to ongoing concerns over the debt problem in europe and a faster economic expansion in the Us compared with the eurozone. ##### Investment ActIvIty macroeconomic drivers tend to lead investment activity in industrial commodities, including copper. This has continued to remain the case so far this year, and macroeconomic events, perceptions and a

nticipations have largely outweighed fundamentals in driving price and volatility. Having had a net long stance over much of the first half of 2012 (according to the cFTc managed money category), an intensification of eurozone woes and fears over the chinese economy led investors into a net short position in late-may. This position was sustained over the summer months and, after trading in excess of $8,000/ tonne for much of the first half, copper prices settled within a lower range of $7,200-$8,000/tonne over this period. an improvement in appetite for riskier assets subsequently saw investors move to a net long position in late august 2012. This came on the back of expectations for, and the subsequent announcement of, further stimulus measures in china and a fresh round of quantitative easing in the United states. However, the improvement in sentiment (and prices) proved to be shortlived, as the focus returned towards sluggish growth and concerns over the impending Us “fiscal cliff” (see chapter 2). consequently, such positions were gradually wound down from early October and investors thereafter moved to a net short position from mid-November, leading prices back below $8,000/tonne, from the mid-september highs of over $8,422/tonne. more recently, hopes for a recovery in Us and chinese demand has once more seen investors establish a net long position and helped prices back above $8,000/tonne in early December. Whilst we acknowledge that there remain significant uncertainties surrounding the prospects for global growth, our base case scenario continues to assume a modest improvement in the economic environment over the start of 2013, assisted by the adoption of loose monetary policies in key countries. as a result, we expect that a long side bias will be maintained over the first half of 2013, which would lend some upward momentum to prices. ##### consumptIon With the demand and wider economic environment remaining uninspiring, we have again made downward revisions to our consumption forecasts from our previous report. For 2012, we now project usage to rise by just 1.3% year-on-year, lowered from our previous projection of a 2.4% rise. This represents the lowest rate of growth in three years, driven by a slowdown in economic growth and ongoing destocking at the downstream level. **5** 3-Year COPPer FOreCast - DeCember 2012 confidential - not for distribution

Usage was particularly weak over the first half of the year, with global offtake falling by 0.6% year-on-year, as a sharp decline in the mature economies’ usage was met by an easing of demand growth in the Brics. although demand thereafter showed signs of stabilising, and year-on-year growth is expected to be recorded over the second half, any recovery has been limited in scale as ongoing concerns over the eurozone debt crisis, the Us “fiscal cliff” and weak chinese demand continued to weigh on activity and sentiment. We continue to forecast that 2012 will represent the low point in terms of consumption growth rates, as the adoption of further, broad quantitative easing in key economies drives a modest improvement in global growth. importantly, a forecast uptick in chinese demand growth is crucial to this trend and, consequently, we have been encouraged by more recent data emanating from the country (see chapter 2). meanwhile, our base case forecast also assumes that Us policy makers will reach a deal to prevent the drastic automatic tax increases and spending cutbacks of the fiscal cliff, helping to support demand in the world’s second largest copper consumer. However, unsurprisingly, we have taken a more cautious stance on the outlook for demand in the eurozone and do not expect positive growth to be restored in that region until 2014. Overall, global consumption is expected to rise by 3.1%, 3.5% and 3.4% in 2013, 2014 and 2015, respectively, taking usage to 22.067 million tonnes in the final year of our forecast period. ##### productIon Global copper mine production is expected to reach 16.346 million tonnes this year, up 2.0% on 2011 but down from 2.2% in our previous quarterly. looking forward, global production capability is expected to increase significantly, with a number of new projects and expansions scheduled for commissioning. Our adjusted base case estimate is for growth of 4.5% a year over the next 3 years; this would bring total mine production to 18.6 million tonnes by 2015. Our adjusted mine production forecast now implies a slowdown in the rate of growth towards the end of our forecast and this is a function of the increase in disruption allowance we attribute to longer-term projections. This conservative approach in part reflects the experience of recent history and the fact that copper mine production has tended to underachieve. We are also increasingly of the view that the global project pipeline is at risk from a shift in the mining industry approach from one of growth and capital expenditure to one of constraint and cost control. This pattern of projected mine supply also implies an acceleration in global refined production over the second half of this year. For 2012 as a whole, our forecast is for output to grow by 1.9% to 20.025 million tonnes, down from 20.271 million tonnes previously. Thereafter, our forecast remains mostly unchanged, with a step up in the g

rowth rate during 2013 and 2014 to 3.8% and 4.1%. We expect global production to reach 22.246 million tonnes by 2015. in the concentrate market, we believe our projections for an increase in supply could lead to higher treatment and refining charges for 2013. However, we note that there is no shortage of smelter capacity and further additions are expected in the near-term, particularly in china, which could temper some of the upside pressure. We are also assuming sluggish growth from the secondary market over our forecast period on the back of weakness in industrial output from the major economies, and as some of the support offered by elevated price levels eases. **6** 3-Year COPPer FOreCast - DeCember 2012 confidential - not for distribution

ECONOMIC ASSUMPTIONS ##### IntroductIon Thomson Reuters GFMS’ views for the forecast period are presented in the form of three probability-weighted scenarios, namely the Base Case, Scenario B and Scenario C. ###### THE BRICS 

We have made further downward revisions to our forecast for the BRICs’ copper consumption this year, and now forecast growth of 3.6% (revised from 4.8% previously). We have lowered our demand forecasts for all countries within the group, the largest of which, in tonnage terms, is to our forecast for Russian offtake (-65,000 tonnes).  This is a result of the sharp downturn in demand for its wire rod, most notably from its key trading partner, the EU-27. Elsewhere, our recent research trip to China uncovered that the much-anticipated uptick in demand growth there has failed to materialise to any significant degree, although recent data provide hope that the economy may have bottomed in the third quarter, whilst offtake in Brazil and India continues to underperform expectations. 

We continue to expect demand growth amongst the BRICs to rebound in 2013, by 5.3%, as the global economic environment improves and as some of the policy easing measures announced in China begin to have a positive impact on consumption in the world’s largest consumer. Thereafter, although we expect that the BRICs’ demand growth will continue to outperform the mature economies’ average, the rate of increase will slow to 5.2% and 5.0% in 2014 and 2015, respectively.  This is in large part a function of a slowdown in the speed of increase in Chinese demand, as the country continues to transition to a slower rate of economic growth.  In the final year of our forecast, total usage amongst the BRICs is forecast to stand at 11.390 million tonnes, accounting for 51.6% of the global total.

In **russia** , copper usage is expected to shrink this year after reaching a peak of 712,400 tonnes in 2011.  Last year’s total represented the highest level seen since the collapse of the former USSR, buoyed by the re-introduction of an export tax on copper cathode in 2010, which led many Russian producers to process refined copper into copper wire rod and then export this product. Indeed, cumulative shipments of wire rod declined 1.1% over the first nine months compared to the same period of last year. Throughout the period, concentrate output accounted for the bulk of global production. This is due to the fact that regions where copper is mined often do not enjoy the labour and energy cost advantages related to refining. More importantly, refining operations are often set up in key consumption centres. The above is clear when comparing the regional split of mined and refined production in 2011. For instance, although 45% of mine production was sourced in Latin America, less than a fourth of global refined production came from the region.
